written.q: Define cloud management and software deployment. (4 marks)
written.a: Cloud management is the process of controlling and monitoring cloud computing resources, storage, networks, applications, security policies and user access so that they are available, secure, efficiently used, monitored and cost-effective. Software deployment is the process of making an application available to users: develop, test, package, deploy, monitor, update/scale.

written.q: What is Infrastructure as Code? Give two tools and four benefits. (6)
written.a: IaC manages infrastructure through code files instead of manual configuration (write, review, deploy, monitor). Tools: Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, Azure Resource Manager, Ansible. Benefits: repeatable deployments, fewer configuration errors, faster creation, version control, better team collaboration.

written.q: What might happen if an application has no load balancer? Describe three types of load balancing. (7)
written.a: All traffic hits one server; under load it becomes slow or unavailable, and it is a single point of failure; horizontal scaling is impossible. Application LB: layer 7, routes by URL path, hostname, headers, content. Network LB: layer 4, routes TCP/UDP traffic by IP and port, high performance, low latency. Global LB: distributes users across geographic regions to cut latency and survive regional failures.

written.q: Why is auto-scaling useful during unexpected traffic increases? State two challenges. (5)
written.a: It adds instances automatically when metrics such as CPU, requests or queue length rise, so the application stays available and responsive without manual action, and removes them afterwards so you do not pay for idle capacity. Challenges: badly configured rules cause instability; scaling takes time; some apps or databases are hard to scale; sudden spikes raise costs.
Horizontal: add or remove instances (2 → 6 servers); improves availability, preferred in the cloud. Vertical: make one server more powerful (more CPU/RAM); limited by machine size.

written.q: What problem does Kubernetes solve? Describe its architecture. (8)
written.a: With many containers across many machines, someone must decide placement, restart failures, scale, update and connect them. Kubernetes is a container orchestrator that does this automatically to maintain a declared desired state. A cluster has a control plane (API server: entry point; scheduler: places Pods on nodes; controller manager: keeps actual state equal to desired; cluster database: stores state) and worker nodes (kubelet: runs and reports Pods; container runtime: runs containers; kube-proxy: networking for Services) that host Pods.

written.q: Explain Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret and Namespace. (6)
written.a: Pod: smallest deployable unit with one or more containers. Deployment: desired number and version of instances. Service: stable network access to a group of Pods. Ingress: external HTTP/HTTPS access. ConfigMap/Secret: configuration values and sensitive data. Namespace: separates resources within a cluster.

written.q: What is a Pod? Why does Kubernetes schedule Pods rather than containers? (6)
written.a: A Pod is a thin wrapper around one or more containers that share one network namespace (one IP, talk over localhost) and optional storage volumes, are always co-scheduled on the same node, and are ephemeral. Kubernetes uses Pods because they explicitly group containers that must run together, give tightly coupled helpers a shared network identity, and let cooperating containers share volumes without extra plumbing.

written.q: Explain the sidecar pattern and the init container with examples. (6)
written.a: Sidecar: a helper container in the same Pod as the app, e.g. the app writes logs to a shared emptyDir volume and a fluentd log-shipper reads and forwards them; teams can change each independently while they still scale and schedule together. Init container: runs to completion before app containers start, e.g. wait-for-db loops nc -z db 5432 every 2 s and the app starts only after the database is reachable; multiple init containers run in order.

written.q: Describe the Pod lifecycle phases and the three restart policies. Does restarting a container recreate a deleted Pod? (8)
written.a: Pending (accepted, waiting for scheduling/images), Running (bound to a node, at least one container running), Succeeded (all exited successfully, no restart), Failed (all exited, at least one with error), Unknown (state cannot be confirmed, lost contact with node). Policies: Always (default, web servers), OnFailure (restart on non-zero exit, batch jobs), Never (one-shot). Restarts happen in place with growing backoff (CrashLoopBackOff). No: if the Pod is deleted or its node fails nothing recreates it; a controller such as a Deployment must do that.

written.q: How can an organisation reduce unnecessary cloud costs? Why design for failure? (6)
written.a: Auto-scaling, shutting down unused resources, right-sizing instances, reserved/discounted pricing, monitoring usage with budgets and alerts, storage tiers, removing unused disks/IPs/snapshots, serverless for suitable workloads. Design for failure because in large systems failures will occur; using multiple AZs, no SPOFs, load balancers, replication, automated recovery, health checks, backups and tested DR plans keeps the service running.
